title: Kerala HC Dismisses PIL Challenging Women-Only 'Freedom at Midnight' Event
excerpt: The Kerala High Court refused to entertain a petition challenging men's exclusion from a women-only Independence Day eve celebration in Thiruvananthapuram, calling it 'slipshod' and devoid of valid materials.
body:
• Kerala HC refused to entertain a PIL challenging men's exclusion from the state government's "Freedom at Midnight" event held on Independence Day eve
  • The event, organized by the Department of Women and Child Development, ran from 10 PM on August 14 to 1 AM on August 15 in Thiruvananthapuram's Thampanoor area
  • The State clarified that restrictions applied only to the women's conclave — public roads remained open to all
  • The Court found the petition was based on unverified press reports and filed in a "slipshod manner" without first approaching authorities

The Kerala High Court on Thursday refused to entertain a public interest litigation challenging the exclusion of men from the state government's "Freedom at Midnight" event — a women-only celebration held on the eve of India's 80th Independence Day in Thiruvananthapuram.

The Event and the Challenge

The program, organized by Kerala's Department of Women and Child Development, was scheduled from 10 PM on August 14 to 1 AM on August 15 along the stretch from PMG Junction to Overbridge Junction in the city's Thampanoor area. It was designed as a symbolic initiative allowing women and children to safely reclaim public spaces while marking the anniversary of Indian independence.

https://x.com/barandbench/status/2088228341094744285

Adarsh SR, a social activist and lawyer, filed the PIL expressing apprehension that men would be prohibited from entering certain areas during the program. He argued the restrictions would violate Article 14, which guarantees equality before the law, and Article 19(1)(d), which protects the right to move freely throughout Indian territory.

The Court's Response

A Division Bench comprising Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice Syam Kumar VM was not persuaded. The Court first noted the State's submission that restrictions applied only to the women's conclave, not to public roads in the area.

"The learned Special Government Pleader on instructions has submitted that there is a restriction for the entry of men to the conclave alone, which is a program intended for women and children, organised by the Department and the transportation and use of the relevant road by men is not intended to be impeded in any manner."

— Kerala High Court order in Adarsh SR v State of Kerala

The Bench faulted the petitioner for not approaching the concerned authorities before seeking judicial intervention. It noted that no writ of mandamus would lie unless the aggrieved person first approaches the relevant public authority — and that the right to invoke PIL accrues only after non-consideration or rejection of such a representation.

Most pointedly, the Court found the petition entirely lacking in substance.

"We note that averments have been made in this writ petition without any basis and devoid of any valid reliable materials. A Public Interest Litigation is not to be filed in such slipshod manner. Such petitions are not maintainable."

— Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice Syam Kumar VM

The Court declined to interfere with the event in any manner. Special Government Pleader Sreelatha Parameswaran appeared for the State.

Women's Safety and Public Spaces

Kerala's "Freedom at Midnight" initiative fits into a broader national conversation about women's safety in public spaces — particularly after dark. Across Indian cities, women routinely avoid public areas at night due to safety concerns. The Kerala government's approach of creating a dedicated women-only zone during the Independence Day eve celebrations was an attempt to address this gap through an affirmative, celebratory framework rather than restrictive measures.

The Court's refusal to entertain the PIL effectively signals that such targeted empowerment initiatives do not automatically breach equality guarantees under the Indian Constitution, provided they do not impede others' fundamental rights — a distinction the State clearly drew in its submissions about public roads remaining open.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For NRIs who follow India's evolving social landscape, the case touches on a familiar tension: how far can the state go in creating women-only spaces? India's Article 15(3) explicitly permits the state to make "special provision for women and children," and courts have consistently upheld affirmative measures under this provision. The Kerala HC's dismissal of this PIL reinforces that judicial framework, while also tightening the bar for frivolous PILs — a concern Indian courts have raised with increasing frequency.

The ruling joins a string of recent Kerala HC decisions on women's rights, including a July 2026 order upholding the state's free KSRTC bus travel scheme for women and transgender individuals under the Priyadarshini scheme, where the Court cited Article 15(3) to affirm that "economic empowerment of women cannot be subjected to judicial review."

What's Next

The event proceeded as planned on Independence Day eve. The ruling, while specific to this case, adds to growing judicial precedent around women-only public initiatives in India. It also serves as a reminder to would-be PIL filers that courts expect substantive materials and prior engagement with authorities before entertaining such petitions.
nri_angle: The ruling reinforces India's constitutional framework for women-only public initiatives, relevant to NRIs following evolving social policy and women's rights in India.
